title: Introduction to Matplotlib and Figure Structure
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Introduction to Matplotlib and Figure Structure.
Select appropriate Python library operations for the analytical question.
Inspect inputs, data types and intermediate results before interpreting output.
Validate calculations and communicate results with suitable evidence.
Identify assumptions, edge cases and limitations in the analysis.

understand.concept: Matplotlib is a Python plotting library. A Figure is the overall drawing canvas and an Axes is the area that contains data, ticks, labels and legends. The object-oriented interface uses fig, ax = plt.subplots() and methods on ax. Separating data preparation from plotting makes charts easier to test, reuse and customize.
understand.whyItMatters: Reliable data analysis requires choosing operations that match the question and checking how transformations affect the evidence. Clear methods make results easier to reproduce, explain and review.
understand.analogy: Think of an analysis as preparing a carefully labeled report: organize the records, calculate the measures, and present the evidence. The analogy is limited because real data requires explicit validation and statistical judgment.
understand.summary: Introduction to Matplotlib and Figure Structure extends the Python data-analysis workflow with practical, reproducible techniques.

explain.narrative: Import Matplotlib, create a Figure and Axes, add data with an appropriate plotting method, label the chart and save or display it in the target environment. In automated or server environments choose a non-interactive backend before importing pyplot. Close figures in repeated batch jobs to avoid accumulating memory. A chart should communicate the data rather than decorate it.

examples.title: Create a figure and axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
print(type(ax).__name__)
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: subplots returns a Figure and an Axes object for plotting.

examples.title: Add a line to an axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6])
print(len(ax.lines))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: plot adds one line artist to the Axes.

examples.title: Set a title and axis labels
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set(title='Weekly visits', xlabel='Week', ylabel='Visits')
print(ax.get_title(), ax.get_xlabel(), ax.get_ylabel())
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Titles and axis labels explain what the plotted values represent.

examples.title: Save a figure to memory
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from io import BytesIO
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2], [3, 4])
buffer = BytesIO()
fig.savefig(buffer, format='png')
print(buffer.getvalue()[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n')
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: savefig writes an image; an in-memory buffer avoids creating a persistent file in this example.

examples.title: Create two separate axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
print(len(axes))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: subplots can create a grid of Axes for related views.

practise.guidedTask: Create a Figure and Axes for a small business dataset. Add a chart, title, axis labels and a legend, then save the result to a PNG file or in-memory buffer.
practise.independentTask: Build a plotting function that receives prepared data and returns a Figure. Keep data cleaning outside the plotting function and close figures in batch workflows.
